new_statements.quote: मानक हिन्दी और बाँगरू दोनों में सार्थक बलाघात की सत्ता शब्द स्तर पर है अर्थात् वाक्य में किसी शब्द पर बलाघात का स्वनिम होने या न होने से तो अर्थ भेद हो जाता है परन्तु शब्द में किसी अक्षर पर बलाघात कम है या अधिक, इस बात से अन्तर नहीं पड़ता। [...] सामान्यतया शब्द में केवल एक अक्षर पर ही बलाघात होता है और मानक हिन्दी और बाँगरू दोनों में ही यह अनुमेय होता है। शब्द के विभिन्न अक्षरों में से किस अक्षर पर अनुमेय बलाघात होगा, इस सम्बन्ध में विद्वानों द्वारा जो विचार मानक हिन्दी के बारे में प्रकट किये गये हैं, वे ही बाँगरू के अनुमेय बलाघात पर भी लागू होते हैं।
new_statements.translation: In both Standard Hindi and Bangru, meaningful stress exists at the word level, i.e. whether or not the stress phoneme falls on a given word in a sentence does change the meaning, but whether the stress on a given syllable within a word is weaker or stronger makes no difference. [...] Normally only one syllable in a word bears stress, and in both Standard Hindi and Bangru this is predictable. As to which of the various syllables of a word will bear the predictable stress, the views scholars have expressed about Standard Hindi apply equally to the predictable stress of Bangru.
new_statements.citation: Bansal, Somdatt (सोमदत्त बंसल). 1981. Mānak Hindī aur Bāṅgrū kā vyatirekī adhyayan [A contrastive analysis of Standard Hindi and Bangru]. PhD thesis, Panjab University, Chandigarh. Ch. 1 Svanaprakriyā, §1.9 Balāghāt, §1.9.1-1.9.2, pp. 95-96.
new_statements.locator: §1.9.1 'sārthak balāghāt śabd star par hī' p. 95 and §1.9.2 'akṣar star par balāghāt anumey' p. 96 (PDF pp. 117-118); Bangru suprasegmental inventory and note 2 quoting Jag Deva Singh on p. 14 (PDF p. 36)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the page images and printed pp. 95-96 of the archive.org scan; archive.org item manak-hindi-aur-bangru-ka-vyatireki-adhyayan confirmed live via its metadata endpoint). Section 1.9 balaghat with subsections 1.9.1 'sarthak balaghat shabd star par hi' (p. 95) and 1.9.2 'akshar star par balaghat anumey' (p. 96) is there, and the two quoted passages read as reported. Minor differences only: the typescript has 'samanyata' where the report normalises to 'samanyataya', writes 'bangru' with anusvara rather than chandrabindu, and carries footnote superscripts (1 after 'shabd star', 4 after 'vidvanon') that the report omits. Footnote 4 on p. 96 is 'Sharma, Aryendra; A Basic Grammar of Modern Hi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive: one syllable per word is stressed and its position is predictable (anumey). Bansal does not restate the placement rule; he says it is the same as the rule scholars give for Standard Hindi (footnote 4 cites Aryendra Sharma 1975, A Basic Grammar of Modern Hindi, pp. 17-18), which in that literature is the syllable-weight rule (stress the heaviest syllable; among equals the rightmost non-final). The 'weight-sensitive' reading is therefore by reference to Hindi, not from a rule spelled out for Bangru; treat as medium confidence. §1.9.3 adds that Bangru's predictable stress is stronger than Hindi's: the stressed syllable becomes heavier (short stressed vowel lengthens, open stressed syllable closes by gemination, e.g. Hindi /moṭā/ vs Bangru /moṭṭā/) and the pre-tonic syllable lighter (unstressed long vowels shorten, initial pretonic short vowels drop), pp. 96-98.
new_statements.exceptions: Bansal rejects syllable-level minimal pairs claimed for Hindi (Mehrotra 1970 /ˈmanā/ vs /maˈnā/; Arun 1961 /ˈgalā/ vs /gaˈlā/, /ˈghaṭā/ vs /ghaˈṭā/) as non-distinctive for both languages (p. 96). The same thesis (p. 14 n. 2-3) quotes Jag Deva Singh (1962-63): stress is not a phoneme in Bangru, but is used for emphasis; Bansal keeps a stress phoneme only for that word-level emphatic function.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (śabd star): stress is distinctive only as sentence emphasis on a word; within the word it is predictable and non-contrastive. Bansal's data are the Bangru of Jind (author's mother tongue), compared with Standard Hindi; no citation-form vs connected-speech distinction is drawn. Sharma 1968 (Central Haryanvi of Meham) lists pitch, terminal contour, juncture and nasality as the suprasegmental phonemes and no stress phoneme, consistent with Bansal.
new_statements.identity_note: Bansal 1981 describes Bangru (बाँगरू) of the Jind district, the core Bangar tract of Haryana, as the author's mother tongue and treats Bangru as a dialect of Haryanvi; Glottolog hary1238 lists Bangaru/Bangri as alternate names, so no separate glottocode applies. Sharma 1968 describes 'Central Haryanvi' of Meham (Rohtak district) and says only palatalization separates it from the Bangru sub-dialect. Ahmed et al. 2026 concerns the Pakistani Haryanvi (Rangri) diaspora variety.

sources.note: Ch. 1 'svanaprakriyā' §1.9 balāghāt (pp. 95-96): in both Standard Hindi and Bangru stress is distinctive only at word level (emphasis on a word in a sentence); within a word the degree of stress on a syllable is not contrastive; normally one syllable per word is stressed and its position is predictable, following the same rules scholars have given for Standard Hindi (fn. to Aryendra Sharma 1975, Basic Grammar of Modern Hindi pp. 17-18); Bangru's predictable stress is stronger than Hindi's, so the stressed syllable becomes heavier and the pre-tonic syllable lighter (§1.9.3, examples pp. 97-98:…

sources.citation: Sharma, Nanak Chand (नानक चन्द शर्मा). 1968. Hariyāṇvī bhāṣā kā udgam tathā vikās [Origin and development of the Hariyanvi dialect]. Vishveshvaranand Indological Series 41. Hoshiarpur: Vishveshvaranand Vedic Research Institute. In Hindi.
sources.note: Phoneme inventory of Central Haryanvi (Meham, Rohtak; author's own speech), pp. 44-46: supra-segmental phonemes are (1) sur/pitch with three levels, (2) āntasur/terminal contour (four), (3) juncture, (4) nasality — no stress phoneme is listed and no word-stress placement rule is given. Diachronic chapters use 'svarāghāt' (accent) only to explain loss/shortening of unaccented vowels (e.g. pp. 104, 163); p. 244-ish notes a special emphatic balāghāt on interjections.
